comments.name: ADN
comments.body: It's beyond bizarre that any professor, let alone one at Williams, could announce so unequivocally that writing isn't necessarily as important as thinking.  Exactly how does Professor Cruz get his words on the page (or the screen)?  I suppose he would say by using "cognitive scaffolding." (And at that phrase I would run for the hills.)  Despite Dr. Cruz's arguments to the contrary, we professional writers do write, as Joan Didion precisely reminded us, to discover what we think.  The act of finding the right words, and then rewriting to make our discovery more clear (or more convincing or more moving) is all about learning what we think.  Writing is a "technology for cognitive offloading?"  Who uses barren pop culture language like this to describe the creativity of putting words together?  Was Shakespeare offloading his cognition?  Rather than writing, Professor Cruz recommends, engage with others to improve your thinking and social relations at the same time?  Okay, now we're into weird.  How about we do both?  Any student who can express his ideas better in class than on paper can only communicate with the people in the room.  What about the wider audience called humanity?  If I may be permitted some cheap snark, I'm awfully glad I chose another of the Little Three to attend rather than Williams. This piece on every level is rather silly.

Per the advanced thinking of that culture - captured in sacred texts and beyond - death is not a terminal event. It is a transformation. And yes, humanity will face that at some point. And so will the airship that is carrying us through this unfathomabe thing called Universe.

On a more relatable note - the biggest underestimation on planet earth has been the adaptibiity and evolution of species, including the homo sapiens. It is laughable to think AI - software running on hardware will take over. All it would take are physical disruptions to power and cooling systems of hyperscalers - that humans built to create AI - to tame the AI 'monster'. Not to mention physical disruptions to key gateways of the global Internet. Sure, there will be great disruptions to life as we know it now, but life will indeed go on and humanity will survive and live out its natural life - perhaps of a few thousand more years! comments.name: Jake Wagner
comments.body:
I would not be an AI enthusiast except for one thing.

The US now has $40 trillion in debt and no easy way of paying that debt off.  Americans live in a dream world in which they imagine they will be able to borrow forever with no consequences.

If past history proves true, that is just plain wrong.  Earlier empires have repeatedly collapsed due to profligate spending.

Yet like Marie Antoinette who wanted "just a few more hours" before facing the guillotine, Americans want an escape hatch.

And artificial intelligence provides a potential escape hatch.

If America gets a monopoly on Ai, then with only 4% of the world's population, the US could continue to produce something the rest of the world is willing to pay for and lending money to the US will seem OK to those who are sufficiently impressed by AI.

Can it last?  Not forever.  But like any Ponzi scheme the point is that it lasts so that present participants can continue to enjoy the pleasures of going ever further into debt.  For a while.

The problem with instilling "morality" into AI is that it will destroy what makes AI work.  And then America faces a Depression II as it struggles to pay off decades of spending on forever wars that were never needed.

I wish America had better choices.  But AI allows the music to keep playing and people to believe America is wealthy.  Just a little bit longer.

US political leaders can have a lot of influence. For instance, Lincoln's arguing that slavery is morally wrong probably helped many people realize that slavery is morally wrong.

However, it would be good if Hamilton were to focus less on his religious beliefs. For one, it's unlikely that God exists. I know of the existence (or likely existence) of a huge number of things, and I don’t know of the existence of God or anything that is even remotely similar to God, for example, an angel. Among other things, I've never seen God or anything that is even remotely similar to God. Analogously, I don’t know of the existence of anything that is even remotely similar to a planetary body with the circumference of the planet Jupiter that is composed entirely of the element gold. And it's unlikely that any such planetary body exists.

In addition, along the lines of a point that Socrates made in The Euthyphro, beliefs are not true in virtue of God believing that they are true. If God were to exist, God would presumably be rational. So, God would have the ability to know that those beliefs that are true are indeed true. Thus, God’s believing that a given belief is true does not make the belief true.

Obviously, there are plenty of reasons to protest it, but as an educator, I think AI has huge potential to help students learn—if we actually scaffold it and set guardrails.

I’d encourage any teacher, no matter what level they teach, to download and at least skim the 2026 Brookings report, "A New Direction for Students in an AI World." 

We also need to be more direct with students about how their brains actually learn (and how AI detectors are mostly a scam!). We need to become much better persuaders of students about why struggling through a hard thinking task is key to building critical thinking skills for the long run, instead of acting like gatekeepers focused only on the final product. I don't think anyone should be using AI to write their papers, opinions or anything that is public facing. We lose the unique voice of the writer - the humanity. And frankly, AI doesn't write grants well - not yet. Hopefully, I can retire before the robot takes my job.

comments.name: Summer
comments.body: It’s a simple moral question of not taking credit for work that is not your own—any academic knows this & it doesn’t matter that AI has “rolled out so quickly.”  Good scholarly writing includes “language refinement, clarity and organization, etc” —these are all intrinsic parts of good  writing, not something separate from it. Yes, they can be hard: Writing is thinking.  The issue is simple and not “murky” at all.  I’m glad I retired just as Chat GPT came on the scene, but I still feel so sad for the culture of academia.

comments.name: W in the Middle
comments.body:
Where does this inchoate idiocy end. Our most skilled surgeons denigrated for using robotic assists? Bespoke tailors to our wealthiest elite boycotted for using machines for part of the stitching, vs threading each one by hand??

As far as Schnell, he is a mathematical biologist (and, at first glance, a very accomplished one) – i.e. words are not his stock in trade as ends, but only as means. It’s very evident from his WaPo essay that the clarity and coherence of his message is more fundamental to him than stylistic flourishes and persuasive phrasing. 

Further, I’d seen this genre of narrative construction decades before any of what we now know as AI even existed.  It was the consistent/cultivated style of speech of the C-levels at what was once one of the most powerful companies on the planet – whether  extemporizing, or giving a meticulously curated keynote at some conference.

For the greatest salesforce on the globe – clarity was the most persuasive of the spoken arts. And not a bot in sight

Also for clarity - so much of this smacks of academic desperation and panic at someone or someones increasingly asking why learning to read, write, and – of course, critically think – takes 4 years and ~$300K, anyhoo

comments.name: Dr. H
comments.body:
“The classic features of A.D.H.D. include things like not staying on task, losing the thread of a conversation and forgetting instructions. They are failures of “sustained engagement.””

By this definition—which I do not intend to contest—do we not all, to some extent, suffer from ADHD in our tech-addled society?

comments.name: Ag
comments.body: “Emotional impulsiveness and low frustration tolerance” - it sounds a lot like our president

comments.name: Alojb
comments.body: The phsyical world of so called "real life" proceeds at a certain frame rate. The online world / computer games / interaction with devices proceed at a different, much higher framerate. The dissonance between these two framerates causes so-called "attention" issues. The brain cannot easily toggle between them. That's my pet theory. It's about a mismatch between when the brain expects the next input to come and when it comes.

comments.name: Gretchen Anne
comments.body: I was diagnosed at 82 and a low dose of Ritalin enabled my being more organized and trying to do six things at once. I now understand why I am the way I am and why I struggled so hard with the stumbling blocks I faced thru life.

comments.name: Bryan
comments.body: It might be interesting to see if there’s a correlation between the rise of ADHD diagnoses and the onslaught of information we are forced to digest from the internet. Might the increase see an uptick around, say, 2005? Moreover, are there differences reported between traditional school environments (lectures, rows of desks, positive reinforcement for sitting still and being quiet) vs. non-traditional school environments like Waldorf, Country Day, or Montessori (which are far fewer in number, granted, but give kids more outlets for movement and, theoretically, a lower teacher:student ratio)?

comments.name: ThinkAgain
comments.body: It's too bad that drugging some kids is the only way to get them to sit in a classroom and try to learn until they get through high school.  Education that required kids to sit down for long stretches premiered in the 1600's but wasn't commonplace in the US until the 1800's.  Some brains are built for this kind of education and some aren't.  The ones that aren't belong to children labeled ADHD etc. Maybe with AI curricula can be developed for them that makes the best use of their aptitudes.

comments.name: Morgan Eeeee
comments.body:
I'm suprised more people do't seem to realize ADHD isn't normally  stand alone condition. It's a prelude to cognitive decline, but the inattention part comes first, decades before the other stuff. Most people have at least low levels of neuro inflammation from various toxins in the environment, water air, food, ect. If it's not exactly toxin induced, then it's immune dysregulation from probably a variety of environmental exposures/triggers and stimuli - this stuff is hard to tease out and impossible to experiment  and test but it still seems like people would understand the general process that's happening. 

Cleaner air, food, and water most definitely help me focus better and for example, when I get exposed to things like mold and VOC's I do lose my ability to focus pretty rapidly. Mold exposure is linked to many physical and MENTAL health problems and it's always been a mystery that the elephant in the room is never addressed when discussing "conditions" like ADHD, which can absolutely be managed and controlled to some degree by controlling your external environment - although not the degree that meds can, fair enough. It's still a giant factor no one is talking about.....

comments.name: JV
comments.body:
I was diagnosed with adhd pretty young. I refused to take medication, I went on strike so to speak, I think I cried at the dinner table and stopped speaking after I said ‘I don’t want to, I’m not broken’. I really thought it meant something was broken in my brain. I learned over time how to manage it- but it took a lot of time. 

There must be some sort of correlation with low inhibition I would think. I don’t know, when I was little I would throw my body around in skiing, gymnastics, soccer, and swimming (those dives!). 

I figured out it was basically what the author says- sustained attention with reinforcement as a type of modifier. I wasn’t good at math (which is funny because my work includes stats which I actually really enjoy) but I learned to read super young and went through books so fast, after I read my parents books I read library books. To this day if someone doesn’t know what to give me for a gift it’s a card to buy books. 

Since I loved reading I had no trouble paying attention. I can  stare at spreadsheets and go over the minutiae of data for hours. But my office looks like- well, people expect it to be nice and tidy, a perfectionist office. It’s definitely not- it’s extremely messy but I know where things are. I do! 

I often wonder if it would not of been better for me to take stimulants. I turned out okay but I guess I’ll never know. By the way, do stimulants make boring tasks more enjoyable? I can’t take them due to health reasons. Just curious!

The cash flow from that oil would go into a "lock box" Government Trust Fund. The Federal government would only spend 3% (the real expected return). At $100/b oil, about $79/b would flow to the GTF. at 100mm b/d would be $3T/year. Norway banked this for 30 years. Its easy to see 10 years putting $30T in the bank, enabling the US to spend $1T of it. THAT is the Nordic model

CENTCOM'S press releases certainly suggest cherry-picking of data sources most optimistic in their projections of net crude-oil barrels passing throug the Strait of Hormuz..a ship/tanker headcount is at best a "crude" approximation of confirmed load, and this numbers game can't be separated from the political objectives, which clearly are aimed at diminishing the strength of Iran's claims of total control over outbound traffic not approved by the IRGC.

Either the stocks of crude are substantially increasing, and downstream distillate products are hitting the markets, or not at levels where we can see improvements, full stop.

comments.name: Mania

I calculated that the electricity cost to travel the equivalent of a full tank is $16 AUD maximum, compared to $100+ for gasoline at the current prices. The car is, quieter and smoother to drive; far superior to fully combustion engine cars with their gear changes and noisy engines. The only drawback is the car is so quiet that I can hear my tinnitus while driving now but I can learn to love having the radio in all the time! I’d recommend your next car be electric.

comments.name: Disillusioned1

It is far too late to try to manage AI just as it is far to late to try to manage bio-engineering.  They cannot be stopped or even successfully regulated  by the U.S. or any national government. Modern science awaits no Luddites.

In contrast, there is plenty of time for prudent states to regulate or even exclude the AI "super data centers" that, unlike typical internet data centers, greedly consume fast quantities of energy and water.  

A proposal that will be considered by Illinois requires data centers to provide their own electricity and water without depleteing others' supplies.  That would work for me.  

Of course, highly evolved states such as Indiana and Texas are welcoming super data centers even though neither state can afford the drains on their electrical and water supplies.  Those states are two examples why I personally fear AI a lot less than I fear Yahoo Republicans.

Visibility means wear something that stands out -- a  safety vest, light clothes at night and use lights front and back all the time. comments.name: Political Genius.

The Princeton professor is asking that we give credence to the opinions from a machine on the economy of 2030 based on 12,000 words written by John M. Keynes sometime prior to 1946?

comments.name: BCBill
comments.body: Puffery, fiction and a trifle. The digitally generated verbiage is no more Keynes than you or I. This is Keynes interpreted by the thoughts and minds of the persons setting the programming parameters. This is a Keynes fixed in time, based on thoughts he generated 80 plus years ago. Who is to know how he would think, if he knew the changes in economic theory and with human society since his death in 1946? This reminds me of "originalist" legal interpretation, of divining the meaning of something by attempting to determine what someone else thought in the past; someone who has not experienced changes that have occurred since they existed. That is more a sophist exercise, than an attempt to ascertain the truth.

comments.name: tara
comments.body:
Very interesting except... it concentrates on industrial automation as a road to great productivity. That began in the early 19th century.
It leaves aside the effects on populations outside the industrial-digital superpowers.
It says nothing about the real 'brain' behind Advanced-gain AI'. Or, about 'monopoly of received knowledge and discourse,' or about liberty and privacy, or why society regulates technical APPLICATIONS and distribution into existing society.
 It still has the robot chained to the workbench. But AI is all about the extension of a new LANGUAGE called digitalization, and, extension of computing speeds in that language. That's called mathematics, linguistics, and communication.
The real modern prophets are 2, and they are both communication specialists and philosophers of an older kind: - the English novelist  George Gissing: New Grub Street, published1891, which literally described how a robotics of future book printing would crush all existing books, and grind their words and phrases into a mash-up, to produce the 'new books' which is the new knowledge. That's AI.
- Marshall McLuhan, who told us why the Medium is the Message.

comments.name: Michael

How does Gates imagine that the controls and safeguards could be implemented at the scale of LLM usage? To have any chance of being effective, the control apparatus would need to be an LLM itself, and vulnerable to the same misalignment as the models it is meant to police. 

Just the mechanics of bot-vs-bot are bad enough as a security protocol, but we have to keep in mind the asymmetry of offense and defense. The defender (safeguard bot) needs to be 100% reliable, while the attacker (current models) only needs to succeed once. Given the probabilistic nature of these models, attackers will tend over time to prevail.

Efficacy in job performance was taboo. The more we spent to get the job done, the larger our next year’s budget. This was among some of the worst fraudulent behaviors I have ever observed. Multiply what I observed by millions and the value of taxpayer money squandered is incalculable… and the amount of inflation induced thereby likely greater than that of any other activity. comments.name: pjc

In our physical space in the US we are shedding at a rapid clip our invaluable "third places" -- places that are neither work nor home, everything from the bowling league to the church picnic to the free people's park, right in the center of town.

On the interpersonal side, it's the personal space itself that has collapsed because we invented digital third wheels.

I'm older and I once asked an equally old friend if they could put their phone away, since we hadn't seen each other in 10 years and well, we were at dinner.

He left very early the next morning, for an afternoon flight. I swear to all of you, all I asked was that he not look at his phone every 5 minutes. He's retired. He has few friends. 

He doesn't want any? Not if it means encroaching on his right to divide his attention. 

Friendship, like romance, is in perilous times. 

And all I said was, "The problems of little people do amount to a hill of beans in this crazy world, so get off the phone."

"Maybe you'll understand some day," I said, as he left the next morning, already scrolling.

Fraternity and sorority houses should be banned, there’s no reason for them except they want privacy to flaunt the rules like hazing and assaults. 
If it’s about networking and philanthropy, then explain the last time your company sponsored beer pong or local Chamber members were arrested for hazing.
Schools should work with local businesses to cut back illegal drinking. If they are adults then make it legal and let them behave responsibly otherwise if it’s illegal then make the consequences a deterrent. 
Offer alternative activities. Sober dorms.

Some of my best experiences were in little tiny towns and stops along the road. If I had it to do over again I would still go on rental car and maybe take a couple train trips from a city for that experience too. My wife and I biked around Ireland for our honeymoon; 1984.  We flew from LHR to Cork, then started out from there, to ride the East coast, Dingle Peninsula on our own bikes.  We "kissed" the Blarney stone too.
Beautiful scenery, and while we carried camping equipment  on our bikes, small mountaineering tent, gas stove, sleeping bags, it rained every afternoon, so we spent most nights in a BNB to dry out our gear.
Next morning  head out again, ride in the rain..
Camped out (one of the few times ) on a peninsula near Baltimore, and met two French sisters from Brittany.
 A great way to see the countryside..but you want bike repair kit.
The following summer, on a solo bike trip in France, I met one of these sisters at a roadside market in Provence ! I was on the same bike, wearing the same rugby jersey. She looked like she had seen a ghost.

comments.name: Theresa Lee
comments.body:
I have non smokers small cell lung cancer.  I have never smoked. I am 70 , very fit, and was diagnosed stage 4 metastatic in March, 2026.

It was in my lungs, liver, lymph nodes, bones - with too many lesions to count.  I had 34 lesions on my brain. 

My oncologist ordered gene testing and I was a good candidate for a targeted gene therapy pill called Tagrisso.  I took Tagrisso and now in October, 2026 all but 1 of the 34 brain lesions are gone.  My liver lesions are almost gone.  My bone lesions are almost gone.  Most lymph nodes register close to normal.

My cancer is still considered aggressive but without Tagrisso , I would already be dead.

Aside from fatigue and nausea, I actually feel pretty good.  I have resumed working out and “living my life”.

These targeted gene therapy drugs should be available to all.  Thanks to Joe Biden,  our prescription bill outlay was capped at $2000.  I am on Medicare and the Tagrisso is now no cost to me every month.  Otherwise, Tagrisso would be $20,000 a month.

I’m living proof this therapy works.

The Fed's years-long attempt to ensure low risk in the U.S. housing market is a direct cause of 2008's world-wide catastrophe.

The banks' lending wasn't problematic; they understood the risks, and quite seriously would have been OK with losing their collective $20BB: you make your bets and you take your chances.  And if the fund's collapse had prompted a sell-off in the A.I. investment market, well, that might have been for the best. And if their lenders' stocks took a hit, well it's not the SECs or the Feds business to ensure that Goldman's and BofA's stocks are good investments.

There will be a reckoning; the Fed and the SEC need to step back and let it happen.

comments.name: Geoffrey Ley
comments.body:
I see a lot of posts here about this being unnecessary due to drones likely superseding manned aircraft.  Manned aircraft are likely to remain an important part of military power for the foreseeable future, although the role of drones will increase.  As a result, we may not need the numbers of these F/A-XX fighter-attack aircraft as would historically have been the case.

As I understand it, there are generally 3 kinds of drones out there:  1) remote controlled, 2) pre-programmed, and 3) wire-guided.  All 3 are currently being used, but have different vulnerabilities and limitations that cannot be easily remedied.  Remote-controlled drones like what the US has historically relied upon can be hacked or jammed in the battlefield, rendering them useless.  They can be remote-controlled by human pilots or AI, but either way, they need access to satellite uplinks that can be jammed.  Pre-programmed drones have little operational flexibility and are typically one-way drones which are destroyed when they strike a target.  If conditions on the battlefield change, they have limited ability to adapt.  On-board AI can improve this, but this then enters the scary realm of allowing computers to decide who lives & dies on or near the battlefield (the SkyNet problem).  Wired drones are increasingly used on the frontlines in Ukraine by both sides due to the above problem.  However, these drones have limited range due to the length of the wire.  Human pilots are still necessary in combat.

comments.name: S Cameron
comments.body: Excellent points about existing laws, but how long will it be before we as a nation realize that we need Rules for AI similar to the Laws of Robotics proposed by Azimov?  You can argue that those were simply narrative for science fiction, but we are now living in a world previously only existing in science fiction.  Those rules all focused on the safety of humans and humankind.  Perhaps we are already too far past that point to reel it back in because we already have AI killing people on the battlefield and we have people with evil intent who use this amazing technology destructive ways.  Battlefields and bad actor humans will always exist, so we need rules to address them in the same way that we used to have nuclear non-proliferation agreements.

comments.name: Thomas Dillon
comments.body: A safety model exists in the federal government for AI model development. The F.A.A. reviews data from airplane manufactures for a model and decides whether or not the airplane is safe to fly. The federal government needs to be staffed with A.I. experts on A.I. and they need to decide whether or not a model can be released. Continuous learning will be necessary for both the manufacturers and regulators.

comments.name: What
comments.body: Wow, what a crazy idea. You mean there are laws on the books, such as anti-trust, gee I didn't know that. If you didn't notice there is this party in charge that doesn't follow the law, it breaks it.

comments.name: Brooke
comments.body: Excellent takedown and overview of the situation. Forty yrs of 'government is the problem' as the GOP mantra has led us to this precipice. These 'unelected' tech titans need to be reined in and made to face the reality of living in a civilized society. I can hear Bill Gates applauding in the background. We have a lot of work to do to overcome forty yrs of propaganda. I beg to differ w Gates, as I do think the data center backlash is the glass breaking and the public is waking from their tech drugged nap. Hopefully, this will allow cross-pollination of ideas and participation in the social conversation again so we can have a smoother transition into the future.

comments.name: Sweet Sue
comments.body:
Somehow Big Tech has hoodwinked the public and many administrations into thinking that their business is so special, it should not be regulated. Lina Khan and others have deflated that conceit, easily, and shown that there are many tools that can be used to protect citizens from their harmful products.

 Holding corporations of all stripes accountable has been in short supply for many decades. With AI/SI the clock is ticking. We know the trump regime will do nothing, but if the Dems get a leg up, it will be an opportunity to show that they can lead on this important issue.  Hope they're up to it.

comments.name: Maryland Chris
comments.body: Someone else in the comments section has correctly noted that regulation and laws only come into effect after a disaster has occurred. It will be the same for AI.

comments.name: Walter
comments.body:
The weakness of this opinion is that it assumes reactive, fragmented laws can adequately address frontier-model risks before harm occurs. AI is moving very fast, and for many of us, that is a great thing.

In the olde days, lawmen were quick to reach for their guns. Today, enforcement moves slowly; court calendars are backed up for years, and the law is often outdated and fragmented. Tech companies have more resources, talent, and commitment than their opponents... and, in some cases, even than governments. 

Microsoft alone has a market capitalization greater than Australia’s entire annual nominal GDP.

Nor should we assume that tech companies will remain headquartered in the United States. Why not reorganize in Singapore, the UAE, or even establish an orbital headquarters? Self-regulation is better than no regulation.

comments.name: Invictus
comments.body:
As a point of historical reference that seems analogous, the Securities & Exchange Commission was established only AFTER the calamitous Crash of 1929.

If past is prologue, we can expect that same kind of timeline with A.I. regulation.  And when the A.I.-related catastrophe happens (it's not an "if"), much like the '29 crash, many, many people will lose many, many billions of dollars (even trillions perhaps) 

Catastrophe shouldn't have to precipitate a regulatory framework, but it seems to always be that way.  We are kidding ourselves if we think this will end well for any of us. History always repeats itself and sometimes on 100-year cycles. 2029 is just a few years away

comments.name: Casual Observer
comments.body: Making steel has a long history. It’s an alloy of iron and carbon with trace minerals that give it strength and resilience that iron does not have. But the challenge has always been to remove impurities that make the steel fracture under stress. Reliable steel required a great deal of effort and could not be provided in large pieces. Then the processes were developed to produce excellent steel in 40 ton lots and it transformed the world. But making steel requires massive facilities and huge sales to keep it going. In the 1970’s all the old open hearth factories became obsolete all at once by massive sales of steel made in superior ways by foreign companies using technologies developed here by not implanted. Since then, making steel here has become too costly to give investors a good return in a timely manner. Trump’s tariffs cannot change that. A few plants that serve a specialized purpose are feasible but the kind of production that ended half a century ago is not coming back. Trump is somebody who talks before he thinks.

comments.name: Two Cents

This article only talks about the rate of change in crime statistics (e.g., "down 22 percent"). Nowhere does it mention the actual *levels* of crime per capita.

This can be very misleading. For example, if one year there was (magically) only one murder in the U.S. and the next year there were two, the murder rate could be said to be "up by a staggering 100%".

This form of exaggeration is common in discussions of many complex topics involving statistical trends. People probably do it to give their arguments more weight. No doubt it contributes to the general misinformation and chaos.

comments.name: Brian Kane
comments.body: All I can say is "WOW"! As someone who's been grinding away as a freelance journalist and longtime books and film critic profiling both writers and filmmakers for many years I always bear both heartfelt admiration and jealousy that another bloke has gotten the assignment and then done it brilliantly nailing his subject and conveying their essence right down to their marrow. In a way it's like peeling away the layers of an onion digging gently for without tearing and violating the writer's trust and privacy. Janet Malcolm famously warned about us journalists and then biographers being akin to burglars riffling through their subject's dresser drawers. Fortunately, writers like Giles Harvey allow their readers access into their subjects lives without betraying them like mere gossip columnists. His profiles on Alan Hollinghurst, Cynthia Ozick and Alice Munro stand the test of time. This portrait into Sebastian Barry's soul and his work reminds me of two quotes. Tolstoy's opening of Anna Karenina: "Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way ". And Faulkner's warning:"The past is never dead. It's not even past." Keep up the great work GILES!

comments.name: Ellen
comments.body: I would like him to write a biography of his father. All the accolades he received by strangers, friends, and family; yet the misery he inflicted upon his immediate family...his prey. This is a story all too familiar to the women who live with shame all their lives.

comments.name: Bedora
comments.body:
Being a victim of incest myself, I was immediately caught up with Barry's traumatic response to bathing his twins.  This seems very telling of having suffered your own trauma.  Though he may not remember, his father was most likely (at least) inappropriate with him also.  

I can attest to the fact that a child will shove those memories down so deep that it can take decades to surface.  When my memories were coming back in my forties, I thought I was losing my mind.  Why?  Why was I feeling these panics and dissociations that did not seem to make sense?

Generational sexual abuse rolls down though the ages, touching all.

comments.name: Beato Fyde
comments.body:
“It’s the creative wound from which so much has come,” Foster said to me. “And I think to cauterize it in a novel might stop the process.” Barry, for his part, was “thrilled” that Bouguereau had taken his attention. “It meant I could postpone that discussion with my soul.”
I’m glad Foster used the word “might” because “cauterize” is an assumption that’s not at all certain. 
Barry may be inspired by the astonishing recent movie in which Andrew Scott’s character has revelatory and healing conversations with his parents … 30 years after their deaths.

comments.name: Nb
comments.body:
"What big, loud talking fools are fathers sometimes." This line alone is worth the price of the paper. 

I appreciate the way this piece shines light on the dilemma of those who are adjacent to the abuse -- neither abuser nor abused, but witness, confessor, or intuitive. 

How lucky we are that Barry writes and publishes. How lucky we are that there are journalists who write such thoughtful and caring pieces. 

Every time I read intelligent and generous writing I feel that I am given a lifeline to a literary world that seems to grow ever smaller and more endangered in these dark times.

Bravo, encore une fois.

Permit me to suggest another Giles Harvey piece from December, 2024: "What Alice Munro Knew".

comments.name: Chan Jit Loon
comments.body:
AI, beyond the final frontier of human intellect, can do good or harm to humanity, beyond our imagination. We underestimated the long term harmful effect of oil, and, it is much easier to underestimate/imagine hyper super AI risks. 
Power without control is dangerous. But too much control stifles creativity, entrepreneurism, passion, etc, the one critical lead that America enjoys over others. Too little is disastrous. As usual, it is always a balance of regulations and freedom, for the good of humanity.  Fortunately, the AI CEOs and scientists, etc are aware of their awesome powers and responsibility, and, intend to use AI for the good of humanity. They also know their creation can  unintentionally destroy humanity and themselves. 
Beyond laws, it is the moral character of the players that is the real determinant.  Therefore, Trump's light moralistic declaration for responsibility pledge is good, for this moment. May I suggest Americans be more educated on AI usefulness, and, risks, to improve their daily life, business, etc.  I hope for positive AI success soon on discovery of cancer cures, weather, quality education, energy, etc. Testing and controlling their AI models for safety, is a difficult, expensive and needs imagination.  Therefore, AI companies should cooperate to formulate, comply and share protocols and facilities on testing, AI risks and control lessons, similar to the FDA drug testing. We hope for a safe, accessible and powerful AI for the good of humanity.

GOP supporters will point to his mastery of everything, including AI. They celebrate the disruption of climate science, including the halting of work by hundreds of scientists on the congressionally mandated National Climate Assessment.  The risk is that future generations will inherit out of control AI, higher debt, weaker legal protections, lost scientific capacity, greater climate exposure, and alliances that no longer trust America to keep its word. LW1: For about 10 years, I organized a girls' weekend of my college friends at my family's shore house. I'd solicit ideas from the group if there were any places they wanted to eat, spas they wanted to visit, snacks I wanted them to have on hand, and the overwhelming response was *crickets*. So I started just booking restaurants I wanted to eat at and spas I wanted to visit. If no one else has an opinion on the plan, we're going to do what I want. 

I tell this story to say I understand your SIL completely. She's taking on all the planning because no one else is suggesting anything better. Your FIL's birthday is the same day every year. Don't act surprised when someone makes a plan.

Strikes me as passive-aggressive behavior.     If it is indeed a power struggle,  I would suggest the writer take some power back.  Next time,  politely decline the sister-in- law's invitation.

comments.body:
let me reframe story no. 1 (as someone who has moved her mother in and is her mother's primary caretaker)

my darn sister never reaches out to me to coordinate any care or event for my mom.  the one thing she does is invite us to "movie night". but my mom cant chew the pizza, has poor vision and doesnt actually like movies

if my sister ever does come by, she never texts me in advance, makes no schedule, nor makes a plan. she never brings a my flower, a sandwich, a fun treat or even a jug of milk.

the one thing i have asked my sister over and over is to take my mom out for an hour: to the grocery, the library or to lunch. that has never happened, so i give up because the fights were aweful and unproductive.

so now i make the plan for all holidays, or birthday or vacation trips for my mom. i really cant plan for everyone's calendar.

comments.name: Paul
comments.body:
Wild take on the first letter. I agree that approaching this as though the SIL is a villain is likely to be unproductive, and it is certainly always possible there is more to the story than the details we get. 

But just taken at face-value, it is rude to bring a cake to a party for someone else's child without discussing it first. It's very likely they already have a cake, and unless you are known in the family for bringing baked goods to every occasion, is not something anyone would expect or want from you. 

Then scheduling a jointly-celebrated birthday party on the weekend of the husband's (her brother's) birthday without any discussion, assuming they couldn't possibly have any other plans? 

Again, it's always possible we don't have all of the information, or that the SIL is truly innocently of any intentional rudeness, but these actions absolutely read as rude on the face of them.

comments.name: Joel Fritz
comments.body: I've been fascinated with astronomy since I was in grade school.  Cosmology really grabbed my attention.  I remember spending hours studying the Hertzsprung-Russell Diagram and stellar evolution.  This is great stuff.  We have telescopes that are beyond anything we could build in the 1950s when I was a kid.  Mt Palomar was a huge deal back then, a 200 inch mirror.  The potential for what we can do with telescopes in space hasn't been fully realized by any means.  There's so much cool stuff out there that we don't know about, yet.  Before anyone mentions the poor immediate ROI of things like this, it's important to realize that serendipity is the hot fudge, nuts  and the cherry of seemingly pointless research. comments.name: KJ
comments.body:
Family friends live in a small town and have a neighbor who had a half-dozen chickens, including a rooster. They were beloved pets, until they were mysteriously poisoned. 

It made me wonder what the person who killed this man's birds thinks about the busy highway and train tracks that run through the area. I hope they don't consider dynamite.

comments.name: Hamlet
comments.body:
Similar problem. I live across a busy road from someone who got chickens a few years ago, including what I assume is a rooster that makes a loud 2-3 note crow every 10 seconds when it's active. 

But, I live in a well-developed but unincorporated area, so there are no avenues for recourse. A little ways down the road is an agricultural property with sheep, cattle, hogs and various fowl. Lots of noise, not much I can do. 

Thankfully, I can close my double-pane windows and keep much of the sound out when trying to sleep. But that rooster is doing its thing right now, even as I type.

So yes, the roosters crow early in the morning, along with other birds that chirp. We also have owls that "hoot" late at night, BUT the worst are the vixens (female foxes) that screech louder than ambulance sirens. Maybe the sirens, truck roars & etc. from NYC where I lived for many decades WERE more tolerable?

Didn’t address the fact that a children’s play park was contiguous, often filled with screaming little kiddos, why stop there, ban happy  children too? comments.name: Rukmini Callimachi
comments.body: The rooster appears on signs all over Vermont — on storefronts, on weathervanes and on logos. But increasingly the most rural of towns in America are deciding that the only place they want to see a rooster is as a statute or as an emblem, with the real ones expected to hold their tongues. Join me to discuss what's happening with roosters in rural towns as officials try to legislate what farm country is supposed to sound like.

comments.name: J Rosen
comments.body:
Lee Krasner HAD a magnificent groundbreaking solo show at the Whitney in the 1970s. I know because I was 18 and a full time student at the Brooklyn Museum Art School. It was breathtaking and a complete validation of my own path as a woman painting. 
https://whitney.org/exhibitions/lee-krasner
Don't miss the fabulous book Ninth Street Women!

comments.name: Gail
comments.body: I never really liked abstract expressionism. Much of it looks like wall paper to me. It may be a milestone in art history, but it is like a bad penny that keeps showing  up since I was in art school in the 1970's. I feel the same way about rock music. Just sick of it.

comments.name: LJIS

Why couldn’t Krasner have her own show??
Some things never change.

comments.name: GLENDA FRANK
comments.body: I fell in love with Pollock's paintings when I was an undergraduate in NYC and would visit them for hours.  When I started my play "Little Images,"  about Lee Krasner,  what I discovered  amazed me.  Three years fallow,  the break through series she called Little Images,  and the emergence of a major artist as she continued working and growing for decades, despite crippling arthritis.  Her friendships with other women artists.  Her being called  "Pollock's widow,"  with all that implied.  Two brilliant talents,  supporting each other until his final years when he couldn't  paint and drank heavily.  She tried to get him to visit France, to inspire him, but he was adamant.

comments.name: Lulu
comments.body:
Oh my!  I cannot wait to see this show.  A well-deserved repositioning of a wonderful artist in Krasner, and both artists presented in their own personal timeline.  I love both artists, and have looked for this curatorial approach for a long time.

Things like this, and the regular collections, are why I am a member of the Met!  (that my late father worked there helps too ;-0)

comments.name: artist

https://www.denverartmuseum.org/en/exhibitions/women-abstract-expressionism

Try to find the catalogue, well worth the effort, and accompany with Mary Gabriel's "Ninth Street Women," a history of these remarkable women.

comments.name: Gabby Zwirchitz
comments.body: It is unfortunate to repeatedly watch the media with its inability to remain neutral/unbiased. I wanted to mention a few points you left out. These include, Marshall BioResources points to its clean USDA inspection reports - although you failed to mention that the same two inspectors show up every time and prepare the reports. For years this has been the case, and when other inspectors are present, citations are higher. Also, very recent criminal animal cruelty allegations have been made and a formal request has been submitted to the Wayne County DA’s office requesting an investigation. The employees have to wear hearing protection inside of the industrial metal buildings where the dogs are caged and incessantly barking/crying. That does not sound like “happy” and “healthy” animals. Additionally, you cited a researcher stating they can’t imagine doing away with animal researcher completely, there are many who oppose that view. Lastly, just because we have used dogs to develop drugs in the past, does not prove that we still need to. Which we don’t.

comments.name: Missy Crutchfield
comments.body:
I’m glad The New York Times covered this important issue, and I welcome Congress’s bipartisan effort to end animal testing through the COMPACT Act (H.R. 10522), led by Reps. Nick Langworthy and Mark Pocan. However, several important points deserve to be part of the public record.

First, the article appears to understate the protest’s size. State Police estimates confirmed that more than 1,000 people attended—a significant demonstration of growing public concern.

The article also quotes a McGill researcher saying it is “hard to imagine” not testing on animals. Yet many respected scientists worldwide are not only envisioning a future beyond animal testing but actively developing technologies to make it possible. Their expertise deserves consideration.

The article suggests local residents generally support the facility. Many marchers, however, spoke with residents who strongly disagree. We heard from people who are ashamed these operations are in their community, including former employees and family members who described deeply disturbing experiences.

Finally, the article omitted documented allegations of animal cruelty involving the facility. Allowing Scott Marshall to state that 40,000 animals are “treated just fine” without addressing evidence and allegations to the contrary presents an incomplete picture of a deeply important public issue.

comments.name: April
comments.body:
It’s devastating to realize that in 2026, animals are still used in painful animal experiments. Experiments which fail over 90% in humans! 
We have superior methods and refused to use them. 
 MBR in New York has over 16,000 Beagles right now, amongst other animals, that are treated horribly and then sold to be tested on and killed. How is this allowed?! Scott Marshall and his wife Courtney regal Marshall should be ashamed… Yet sadly, they’re not!  Their greed is greater than their empathy for animals.

comments.name: Laura Trentz
comments.body: This article is missing out some very important information. What about all the scientists that are testing with modern day tools? What about the stat that 94% of what passes on animals still fail humans? What about the fact these horrible company’s are putting things in their ingredients that are harmful to any living thing? What about S org Marshall himself said he knew thing day was coming (it’s long overdue). Animal testing with dogs and cats is archaic and barbaric - do better NY Times.

comments.name: Diane Delfino
comments.body: End animal testing period . There is never a reason to inflict cruelty and harm on  another living being.  One “scientist’s “ opinion says nothing as they are funded by same system that promotes this .

comments.name: Mary Fox
comments.body: I was there, and there were at least 1000 people there as reported by the authorities. To anyone who thinks it's ok to test on animals, I would ask if it would be ok if it were their pet. I'm sure the answer would be no. There is absolutely no difference. For anyone who thinks it is effective, I would say to educate yourself.

comments.name: Dawn Roehrig
comments.body:
Thank you for Covering this story. I was there and there would definitely more than 400 people at the March and protest. To the scientist who can’t see  future without animal testing, the facts remain that 92% of test that work on dogs do not work on humans. There is new technology that is human specific, including AI, models, and organelles that are more transferable to human anatomy. It’s actually very expensive to breed and keep all these dogs. Only to find that the experiments used on them are not transferable.

As for the claims that the dogs are happy and healthy, hounds are known to be packe animals and crave human interaction.  Being kept in solitary cages, without the ability to interact together, is completely against their biology, and in and of itself causes extreme suffering.
There are videos and documentation taken by whistleblowers, who worked inside Marshall BioResources  and reported the abuse,  It wouldn’t take much investigative reporting to trip over the documentation that’s  all over the Internet. I would think and hope that a newspaper of your caliber  would investigate all the facts prior to printing a story.
With warm regards.

We do have some pebblers, though, that constantly barrage us with memes, to the point I was no longer responding and eventually had to tell everyone I didn't need 30 memes a day.  Everyone actually agreed, we were all afraid of hurting each others feelings. And the main culprit cut it to 10 a week. 

Other friends I may not see for months, or even a year or two, and but with FB we're able to keep current on what's going on so we don't just relive the past. Sadly FB has become a challenge with all the nonsense and ads that's on there now.

comments.body: I'm sure this perspective is helpful for people whom it's helpful for. But TBH, this feels like soft science to me. A rock band is hardly an example of everyday friendships and relationships. That anecdote tells us nothing. I've had absent friends with whom I reconnected and we started right up where we left off. And I've had the opposite. It all depends rather specifically on the nature of each person in the relationship and why they may have "drifted apart." So I really don't see any general applications here. It's all rather generic.

comments.name: Constantine Gillespie
comments.body:
I have become selective in my choice of friends and friend time. I want relationships that are low-maintenance, low pressure, nurturing, without burden, and without guilt. 

If I find myself thinking, "I really aught to call him," then I distance myself. If instead I call a friend out of the blue after a year and pick up right where we left off, then I feel safe and lifted. Sometimes I need to "go dark" and I want my friends to honor that space without nagging me.

It works the other way too. I never tire of time with my partner. We can be all over each other one minute, and completely on-task and separated the next, respecting those rhythms effortlessly. They key is to find friendships that are enriching and not burdensome regardless of time and distance.

comments.name: Slana Spur
comments.body: Unfortunately, we will respond to the housing market dilemma like we do with everything else these days—by playing the blame game.  The Right claims its government that’s the problem while the Left claims it’s government that is the solution, when there are multiple factors at work and each straw, added over time, finally breaks the camel’s back.  Instead of trying to understand them (and that the situation in California is far different from that in New Hampshire or Colorado), we fall back on simplistic assumptions.  Bottom line—there are no instant answers, and sometimes everybody must agree first to ante in their preconceived notions to get to play in the solutions game.

comments.name: Mary
comments.body: We need creative ways to house, and we also need to acknowledge that housing DOES cost taxpayers (that comment in the  article is just sloppy). Yes, job growth is a factor so perhaps requiring successful companies to build in less populated, less expensive areas will draw employment and less costly rentals. Yes, prohibit corporations and non-US entities from snapping up properties. Yes, paying a fair wage. AND let's not forget the impact that building high density, high rise buildings have on our once beloved neighborhoods. I woke to a security motion sensor light beaming into my bedroom (and I have black out curtains PLUS shades) at 4am from the now-allowed ADU facing 4 ft from my bedroom. My other side facing my shower has yet another ADU. A total of 8 cars vie for parking. My neighbor, who once had a garden, is now in perpetual gloom from the two 12 story buildings looming over her tiny yard. I am considering moving, being so distressed and depressed over every square inch of vertical space now being hammered, drilled, and cemented over. I once had a neighborhood. When I bemoan its disappearance I am called a NIMBY. As though my blood, sweat, and tears to purchase my tiny house 25 years ago means nothing now. We need balance, not blame.

comments.body:
This is such a tragic loss but, the fact that these two children died at the same time, it is likely not the result of vaccinations.  
The US has a serious problem, not only with vaccine skepticism but, with a distrust of all science.  The educational system has failed your citizens as has the absence of a single-payer healthcare system like in Canada, where profits are not the priority.  
As for those individuals who refuse to accept what science has proven, they shouldn't get to pick and choose in which science they believe.  That means no MRIs or ECGs - or computers, for that matter.  Either science is real or it is not.

comments.name: AZYankee
comments.body: The article states that the bedroom the twin slept in, often reached 100°! That alone puts them at risk for heat related illnesses and dehydration. Possibly even heat stroke. Toddlers are far more susceptible to these complications than adults.

comments.name: Callie
comments.body: There will be no conviction and I'm surprised the prosecutor's office even filed the case. While the circumstances are "suspicious" (the twins dying at the same time and the mother's inconsistency in detailing events around the time of the deaths) the "beyond a reasonable doubt" standard and the need for jury unanimity in a vaccine skeptical community make it almost impossible to present evidence to meet the requirements necessary for conviction. While the prosecutor will call the forensic pathologist the anti-vaxxers will fund an "expert" who will testify that the post-mortem findings could have been caused by an extreme response to a vaccine (to quote Charlie Kirk "prove me wrong") and that will negate the only chance the prosecutor has to get to the required standard of proof. The sole card the prosecutor has are the autopsy findings and to get to "beyond a reasonable doubt" the defense would have to be unable to find a physician-no matter how questionable their qualifications-to testify that the findings are not absolutely dispositive.

comments.name: laurijst
comments.body:
I am very pro vaccine, but I also know that no medical intervention is 100% safe; there are medications that are taken by or given to tens or even hundreds of thousands of people with no adverse effects but it is still possible that a vanishing small percentage may get very sick or even die.

I didn't see mentioned in the article whether the twins are identical or fraternal. If the former then, as a lay person, it makes more sense that they would die at the same time. if the latter perhaps that invites more skepticism. it is my assumption that the prosecution will focus on presenting medical evidence that will convinces the jury that the cause of death could not be the vaccines. if the evidence doesn't meet that threshold then that could be reasonable doubt.

But as this trial goes on there will be people who will come down firmly on one side or the other regardless of the evidence.

comments.name: Suevee
comments.body: Complicated.  If the twins were sick with rotavirus after being vaccinated, that's a possible contributor to natural deaths, possibly by dehydration. But they were both "found" dead at the same time, in the same bed, it seems strange.  We don't know how much of the mother's story to believe, and the father has every reason to try to defend her, so his testimony is not likely to be very reliable.  Poor kids!

comments.name: Fiona
comments.body: I would love to read about the emotional weight of being the medical staff responding to cases of child abuse.  A pair of toddler twins who had once been regular patients on my unit were drowned in a bathtub together this year.  We had occasion to ready ourselves for the resuscitation of a 3-month-old who was run over by a car being driven by a developmentally delayed 12-year-old who had been allowed to drive not by mother of the 12-year-old and 3-month-old but by the stepmother; there was no possibility of resuscitation.  It hurts to take care of children who are abused.  It hurts to work alongside CPS and the courts when they are so non-professional.

comments.name: GG
comments.body: Having the resources to be able to eat 30 different types of plants could presumably mean that you have access to medical care, have less financial worry/less stress and more time for exercise and creative/fulfilling endeavors. Hence, statistically, you would have a longer lifespan with fewer major health problems. Correlation does not equal causation.

comments.name: Bryan
comments.body:
People shouldn't be basing their diets (or lifestyle) on a single sentence, a hashtag or a bumper sticker.  

People, this isn't difficult.

Michael Pollin:
"Eat food, mostly plants, not too much."

comments.name: ed
comments.body: 30 different plants, at least 30 different pesticide treatments. Talk about a cocktail!

comments.name: noah
comments.body:
Most individuals do not eat the proper amount of plants they need daily.

Many people go months without eating a single fruit or vegetable, when in reality, Harvard University studies suggest that adults should consume roughly 400-500 grams of fruits and vegetables per day. Dietary guidelines measure this intake in ¨cup equivalents¨.

Not eating fruits and vegetables can lead to many health problems such as digestive issues, vitamin shortages, and a higher chance of long term health problems like heart disease. Less diverse microbiomes are generally associated with poorer health, gut microbiomes are primarily nourished by fiber, so in theory, eating different types of fiber promotes the growth of different kinds of microbes.

A solution to this dilemma would be people implementing(or more) plants into their weekly diet.. the idea of eating 30 (or more) plants each week  including fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, nuts, seeds, herbs and spices  has taken the wellness world by storm. It has spawned apps that track how many plants you eat and supplements advertising 30 or more plants per capsule or scoop. Eating 30 plants a week, some influencers, podcasters and physicians say, will diversify your gut microbiome and in turn, improve your health. 

That said, research generally supports the benefits of eating a variety of plant foods.

comments.name: Sequel
comments.body:
Declaring an unverified opinion to be a scientifically-validated fact is very easy. 

Persuading consumers that a given pitchman is an "expert" is even easier.

comments.name: Wendy B.
comments.body:
Let me assure you that there is no scientific evidence to support this goal. Sure, eating a variety of fresh fruits and vegetables is likely to support good health, but beyond that? Nonsense. 

You should always filter these nutritional concepts through what your ancestors probably ate. As hunter-gatherers, they ate what was available. Which part of the world supports 30 or more edible plants all year round? None.

comments.name: Bet
comments.body: Yay! More mandates to further destroy the pleasure of eating.

IF someone was really interested in prolonging their life they might consider NGS= Next Generation Sequencing. Some of life is already predetermined by your genes. Makes sense to find out what's in them sooner vs later.

comments.name: Ivan S.
comments.body:
I’ve been a New York Times reader since high school, and am now of retirement age. I inherited this NYT habit from my father, who was an avid Times reader. In my 20s, I would spend winters in the Alps and do backcountry skiing from hut to hut. Every week, my father would mail the Sports and Week in Review sections to me, which I absolutely cherished.

One week, I didn’t have time to read those sections, so I took them along with me on a trek into the mountain wilderness. I have a photo of myself  on skis in the Swiss Alpine wilderness with my big backpack, and the New York Times Week in Review section sticking out of the backpack straps. In the photo, you could clearly see that it was a New York Times Sunday section. I continue to cherish this photo. And, I will guess it was the first time that the Times was read in a hut in the high Alps wilderness. Thank you, NY Times!

comments.name: Kathleen Brady
comments.body:
The problem is that bike advocates like Trans Alt want to measure pedestrian safety in body count, the number of walkers e- bikes killed. They seem to discount pedestrians who  are maimed, broken, and suffer brain injuries from irresponsible bikers. They claim bikers should not be licensed or registered because the police might harass them. So watch the police. Bikers and bikes, like car drivers and their vehicles, must be registered so that they can be held accountable when they do damage. Bikers must know they are at least more likely to be held accountable when they ride on sidewalks, race northbound on southbound lanes, and endanger themselves and others by their reckless behavior.
According to emergency doctors, e-bikes are a public menace. We need to rein them in or ban them entirely.

comments.name: Tal Barzilai
comments.body: First of all, I'm so tired of groups such as Transportation Alternatives crying foul to this.  Since E-Bikes have a motor, they should be considered a motor vehicles.  Just like all other motor vehicles, they should be licensed, registered, and insured without any debate or negotiation on this.  I don't think the real reason they are against this is because of the cost, but more to do with actually being tracked and held accountable and possibly liable for their actions just like all other vehicles with such documents are.  I have always found it irony that this groups claims that bicycles should have the same rights as all other vehicles when using the roads, but shouldn't be subject to the same rules as all others hence the Animal Farm reference.  Seriously, I could never understand why they want everyone who is driving to be subject to follow every letter of the law, but believe that they are exempt from them and should have special treatment when the rest don't get this.  Just because they ride a bicycle doesn't mean that they are above the law or that their needs can outweigh all others especially when it comes to redesigning streets for them especially when they represent a very small group according to a recent study of NYC commuters on the US Census Bureau.  Let's not forget that they have a history of treating traffic lights and signs as decorations in believing that they don't apply to them yet they only seem to complain about drivers who don't follow them.

comments.name: Scratching
comments.body:
Electric bikes are a great innovation, and a way for those unable to cycle to get around efficiently.
Any vehicle that operates on the roads, and has a motor, of any kind, is a motor vehicle. And should be regulated as such.
Perhaps this class of motor vehicle can have its own catagory under which they are regulated, however, they are not bicycles. And, from what I've witnessed, many of those using these electric bikes appear to need some instruction on their safe operation.

comments.name: nikto
comments.body:
We frequently ride in bike clubs for the elderly. Part of the problem is that people who aren't able to ride regular bicycles because of age, infirmity or inexperience try riding e-bikes. Often they choose e-bikes that have throttles, which don't require pedaling. Basically, electric motor bikes.

These e-bikes are usually very heavy and harder to brake and control in tricky situations. When you combine all these factors with the inexperience and/or slow reaction times of the rider, it's a disaster.

E-bikes with throttles that don't require pedaling should be classified as motor vehicles, be licensed and not allowed in bike lanes. E-bikes that require pedaling (that is, the motor is just an assist) should be allowed in bike lanes, as long as they don't exceed speed limits and weight limits.

If a person can't lift their e-bike and put it on a bike rack, for example, it's too heavy for them and they probably don't have the wherewithal to control it in traffic.

comments.body:
Ma Earth already has the perfect FUSION reactor that delivers enough power in 1 hr to meet ALL of humans' demands for 1 yr. It doesn't create dangerous waste to dispose of or use materials that can be made into weapons to be misused by random "terrorists" or wacko presidents. It hasn't raised it's rates in 4,600,000,000 years, is pollution-free and, when it suffers a huge energy spill, we just call it a "nice day".

Our home solar array is 16 yrs old and paid for itself many years ago. It still produces ALL of the FREE electricity needed to power our all-electric home in southern PA and to charge our EV. We can use the EV's huge battery for backup power when/if the grid goes down. We have spent $0,00 in maintenance costs over the life of the array.

Each year, Americans buy 15 to 16 Million new cars at an avg cost of $50,000. In '25, they installed only 6,100 new home solar arrays at an avg cost of $25k. For those who can't afford $25k upfront there are solar leases available or homeowners' loans that can be paid for by utility cost savings.

A wise consumer can see that, instead of a new $50k car (that loses value immediately) they could invest in a $25k solar array AND buy a low-mileage $25k EV. They'd have Free power, a superior vehicle AND insulate themselves from predatory Big Power and from wars started by insane presidents.

comments.name: Alfonso
comments.body:
I've always had mixed feelings about nuclear. It's unavoidably complicated, expensive and wasteful. From the mining of uranium, to processing, to maintaining the plants, and the end waste problem that has never been addressed. However, if it was done correctly, it could have been a planetary and humanity savior.

Light water reactors are foolishness. They were implemented because of military priorities and expediency. Molten salt thorium breeder reactors solve many problems. They were running at Oak Ridge in the late 1960's. They are inherently safe compared to other reactor designs, can breed their own fuel, and they could potentially burn existing nuclear waste.

The other thing I dream about is desalinization. Desalinization on a mass scale takes massive amounts of energy. If we had these nuclear reactors deployed using the heat for distillation instead of using electricity for reverse osmosis, it's a game changer. With additional reactors for electric power generation we could pump water from the Pacific and turn the western US into a garden, rather than using up the Colorado to nothing.

But none of this will ever happen because the US is a dysfunction society, unable to plan and mobilize for the benefit of all of us.  We only optimized to make money for the Oligarchy.

It's all moot anyway.  Solar is now the cheapest form of energy, ever. Effort should go towards solar, off-shore wind, and energy storage, that's the solution.

We had 60 years to do something. Too bad.

comments.name: Dogpatch
comments.body:
For those of you wondering about “backpacks”
 2007 injury here’s a recap:
Number 435.”Holly”, arrived with a yearling cub. The cub was limping noticeably, and it would put no weight on one of his front legs. With impaired mobility, this bear family was competitively disadvantaged. #435 would not visit Brooks Falls to fish and the cub would not be able to flee any threats.

Many people wondered, will these bears survive and will someone help them? Park rangers and biologists will not intervene to help an injured animal. “Bears injured naturally will not be tranquilized for veterinary care” (Katmai National Park Bear-Human Conflict Management Plan, 2006). Injured bears will also not be euthanized unless they pose an imminent threat to human safety. Will they survive? That was something, at the time, we could not answer.

Holly number 435 plus yearling modified their behavior 
#435 reacted to her yearling’s limited mobility by fishing around the mouth of Brooks River where larger, more aggressive bears are less frequently seen. She also appeared to move more slowly to allow the injured yearling to keep pace. By September, 2007, the yearling’s leg had healed. In 2008, the former yearling cub was seen as an independent bear and no sign of the injured leg. He is now #89 (Backpack) a young adult male who is frequently seen on the Falls and Lower River cams.
That was in 2013

comments.name: Robert
comments.body:
My wife just gave a test to 125 freshmen at one of the highest preforming HS in the State.  Students had a multiple choice question asking to convert 42 
 C to F   The choices were 75, 86, 108, or 115.   She had given them both the equation  F=1.8C+32 and  a few data points. 0C=32F, 20C=68F and 40C=104F….Less than 20% of the students got it right…..or take a local road 5 miles long that needs to be upgraded from a 2 lane to 4 lane road. comments.name: Federico
comments.body:
Interesting article, but it bundles together several very different issues: AI-generated political imagery, election deepfakes, autonomous companies, data centers, and existential AI risk, and it treats them as evidence of one overarching policy problem.

The key logical gap is that a government choosing not to impose a broad, preemptive AI regulatory regime is not the same as having “unregulated AI.” Existing criminal, civil, electoral, consumer-protection, privacy, and corporate laws may still apply.

Likewise, an obviously fictional image of Milei as Spider-Man is fundamentally different from a fabricated video falsely claiming that a candidate withdrew from an election. Conflating satire, propaganda, and factual deception weakens the analysis.

The authors also spend considerable time on the risks of deregulation but barely examines the competing risks of overregulation: reduced investment, barriers to innovation, compliance costs, or advantages for established firms.

Argentina’s experiment may prove wise or reckless. But assessing it requires separating these policy questions and testing each on evidence, rather than linking them through anecdotes, political bias, and rhetorical proximity.

The massive state protocol and public spaces granted to Pope Leo XIV’s visit is a clear "two-tier" enforcement of laïcité in French politics and society. The state’s willingness to mobilize millions in public funding for security, facilitate an open-air Mass in central Paris, and overlook direct challenges to secular laws stands in stark contrast to the intense restrictions imposed on French Muslim citizens. If a prominent Muslim figure were to host a comparable large-scale public prayer or openly criticize the republic's laws from a platform at the Élysée Palace, political circles would almost certainly scream Bloody Mary and respond with widespread condemnation, framing the event as a threat to national cohesion and a manifestation of "separatism". This disparity is further highlighted by the ongoing legislative restrictions on Muslim religious expression, such as bans on the hijab in public schools and various public sector environments, which human rights advocates argue target individuals under the guise of neutrality while the state simultaneously accommodates high-profile Catholic spectacles.

"...because humanism positions humanity as a central character."  

To those of us who may not extol nor denigrate religious belief, one has to see, or perceive, an attempt of modern Catholicism to unite our world through our commonalities versus our differences.  Pope John XXIII brought about the Second Vatican council in the early 60s to 'wake up' the world as to what had just happened less than a generation before and during the tenure of his predecessor, Pious XII who had died only a few years before.  The parochial nature of the world then, as now, needed to be examined and changed so the horrors of World War II (not to mention those of WWI), would be eradicated or at least tempered to the point we, as humans, wouldn't self-destruct.
