comments.name: Reagan Westfield
comments.body: I think that grades are actually the most stressful thing out there, waiting for a test score to come in just to FAIL and all of the low homework scores. Grades are so important but they also make you want to pull your hair out, curl in a ball, and cry. In most parents' and students' eyes anything under a high B is failure, even if you try your very best you can’t get that satisfying A+ that you've been wanting. I even set those standards for myself. I do know of people who don't care about grades, but I just can't even think about anything but school unless it's summer, even in summer you have work to do. From 3rd grade to 8th grade school is just everything, homework, essays, and missing assignments, “school comes first”. Once you get into high school there's MORE responsibilities, like a job, homework and a job after school that's hard. How can school come first with all of that important stuff too? That makes it hard to IMAGINE how college is, rent, a job, big test that might end you, that's so much. To sum this all up I think grades cause everyone stress and that the pass or fail system is hard to imagine in my position but would be good for me.

comments.name: Vihaan Modi
comments.body: I care very much about grades. Grades are important because they decide your future and what college you get into. Grades also provide an example of your level of education and knowledge in a certain subject. Grades almost always do not cause me many problems, but when I have a C or a very low B, I get worried and usually get stressed and when this happens I work harder and for a longer period of time and in a few weeks my grades are back to normal. Grades are important and even though The University of Michigan has set a new grade rule of fail/pass, I still believe that grades are important and should not be replaced.

comments.name: Brighton Norton
comments.body: I think that this is a great idea and I understand how much of a struggle and problem mental health is, I love this idea and I think that it will work great because Personally with the current grading system I always feel so pressured to get an A when even B;s would be fine and I can still live my dream future with those grades. I want this grade system because I struggle with lots of stress and anxiety about school and just having it say I'd passed would make me feel so much better because I've always gotten A’s except for 1 B and I’ve always wanted to keep it that way and be the best student I can. I love this idea and I hope it works and other schools and colleges learn about this and commit to this grading system too.

comments.name: Gianfranco Montalto
comments.body: I believe that replacing grades with a fail or pass system can help the mental health of students. I think this because there are a lot of people that will be sad and depressed if they get a grade lower than a one hundred and even more when you go lower down the scale so getting a high B and being upset that you didn't get an A is worse for a students mental health then getting a score that just says pass. So I believe that it is a good idea but there can be some downsides. One of them is a lack of effort as students just want  to pass as o they will do low effort work. I also disagree with Mr Hess as he says that decreasing the workload will be bad. But I believe that if a student is doing bad they will see it as they will get a failing grade so removing them makes college students less stressed and improve faster due to being in a good mental state. And even Mr Hess’s other point of entitlement doesn't make much sense because if they were that entitled they will get a failing grade because of it.

comments.name: Jane Courtin
comments.body: Honestly, the University makes a good point, but how do they know if the students attending the college will do well in adulthood? Not everything in life is going to be easy, and for the things that are hard to achieve won’t be taken away just because they are difficult. By making grades unimportant, you are giving the students a four year (or less) experience of slacking off and doing nothing. Adulthood will be a huge jump from that to taxes, real-life conversations, and managing your time. Taking away grades takes away the motivation of doing your best and putting in your all. I am not saying that tests aren’t stressful and that getting a bad grade can really mess with you, I’m saying that what’s the point of achieving nothing, to then want to achieve everything?

comments.name: Darren
comments.body: I think that the pass/fail grading policy for the University of Michigan is not a bad idea. Eventually there would be an amount of people doing whatever they want and being more reckless because of this and they would care less about how they pay attention. If it first gets introduced I think students are gonna like it and students would feel less dependent on grades but I feel like some people are still gonna feel the urge to feel like they should because they don't know if they are gonna pass or not and it might cause people to stress out even more. I think they should add more of a description and give more details to students if they do use this new grading system or vote if they should, including students but I know people would take advantage of this and feel like their grade no longer mattered. Over time, people would probably realize how much less stress they have and they would stop focusing on only numbers and make room for extra activities but even with this I still believe that people would take advantage of this somehow but it could be a good idea and if they only do it for the first semester it would probably do good and new students would be more relieved and relaxed without grades even if they have grades the next semester.

comments.name: Charlie Silverman
comments.body:
How much do you care about grades, and why? Do grades cause you a lot of stress?

I care about grades because everyone has them and cares about them. If I was the only one who didn't care I would feel left out and it would worsen my mental health. For me grades do not cause lots of stress but for all kinds of other kids it does because they would have strict parents or not have the grades their friends have.

comments.name: Cole Nemer
comments.body: I think the new pass/fail grading policy is a semi good idea. While yes the idea of school being a lot easier sounds good on paper it is not exactly like that. The real world is hard and if you swaddle people who are new adults it is setting them up for failure. I think instead of doing a past/fail policy schools should try to teach students that grades don’t matter as much as students think they do. Students think that the number that they got on a paper is their whole life and that because they failed their algebra test their life is ruined now. For some people a B on an assignment is bad and for some it is amazing. If you keep supporting someone their whole life then that person will never know what it is like to not be supported. As far as younger grades go I think a pass/fail policy is good. It will force students to look less at the exact numbers and more at the overall picture.

One thing I thought MA did far better than any other classic MA-adjacent film is that it capture her as a 14 year old at marriage, having moved from the far less formal family court culture of Vienna to that of Versailles, and more fully portrayed the many levels of hostility to her and the marriage, and that it was far more brightly Rococo. 

The effervescence reminded me of Dolores del Rio's performance as Madame du Barry in 1934.  

MA also delved more deeply into the couple's problem's with procreating and losing children. 

The little scene of the famous family portrait being modified to remove a child was wordlessly perfect, as were the scenes of the Dauphine at table and at her daily levee. 

The film had its weaknesses as have most English-language MA films. This one added some good value to the genre.

comments.body:
LW owes it to her partner to share her deep feelings of ambivalence about becoming a mother. Nobody should ever have unwanted children — that leads nowhere good. But a desire to parent and to parent with someone you love is deeply ingrained (some would say hard-wired) in the species. This is the sort of thing couples discuss openly and which should bring them closer together. Surely the topic of future parenting arises in conversation. What does it even look like to withhold that ambivalence from a loving partner? Misleading your partner is wrong. 

And just because you wait too long to “come clean” about this for you to have kids doesn’t mean it would be too late for him. There’s a BIG difference between the clock on fertility for men and women. If he wouldn’t choose you over fatherhood now, he won’t choose you over fatherhood later. And time is on his side.

One of the most validating conversations of my life happened when I giving birth to my first child.

The OB came in and wanted to confirm I was declining the epidural. I was pretty nauseous and said I was worried it would increase my need to vomit. Then I said as an aside, "And the pain doesn't feel too different from my period anyway, I've been dealing with this for 20 years, I can handle it." 

He replied "Wow! Those must be some bad periods! You're 7cm dilated now." 

It was then I realized where all those years, especially in middle and high school, when I was scolded for being dramatic, my cramps had been on par with advanced labor pains. I wasn't being dramatic all. Giving birth to 9lb baby with no pain meds was marginally worse in the end (the "ring of fire" aspect was the only part that was different) 

I'm happy for anyone this can help.

What about the ReceptivaDX test? I never see that test mentioned in articles about these new tests for endometriosis, and it is being widely used at IVF clinics. How accurate is this test? 

I was diagnosed with silent endometriosis via the ReceptivaDX after years of infertility (but no classic endo symptoms). As you might imagine, I was not eager to undergo invasive laparoscopic surgery when I wasn’t having obvious symptoms. I was placed on Lupron and letrozole (awful) for two months prior to an IVF embryo transfer. I’m currently seven months pregnant, so I’m happy with the outcome.

I had severe cramps from menarche to menopause. 

I’d have been delighted if there had been a test to provide some insight, even with the risk of false negatives or positives.

False positives followed by surgery don’t seem all that terrible given the alternative of starting out with surgery to diagnose the problem.

False negatives also don’t need to be a disaster, as they can be followed up with other testing. The key, as Dr. Hugh Taylor is quoted as saying in the article, is listening to patients.

After finally reaching menopause, I got Long Covid, and started off with a whole new round doctors telling me nothing is wrong, that a little exercise, fresh air, and a better attitude wouldn’t fix.

I’m trying hard not to rage-type …  I’ll stop now, before the flames coming out of my fingertips destroy my keyboard.

comments.name: PWD
comments.body: Insurance has a lot to do with this. I had laparoscopic surgery several times due to infertility due to endometriosis. Yes, I had heavy cramping during periods, but no one ever told me to expect otherwise-ibuprophen when it finally became OTC was a game changer. No one hoping to get pregnant can wait 7 or more years. Whether insurance will cover the minimally invasive and conclusive laparoscopy is THE question.  There is little to no down time, my doctor found that my ovary was completely covered by endometriosis tissue and moved out of position. I have three children and a grandchild now.  Things really haven't changed much since the 1990s, and I am not especially optimistic that a simple test will be the answer needed in time, when a biological clock is ticking. So really, insurance coverage for laparoscopy is the answer for the near and possibly long term.

The slow progress toward better methods of detection is encouraging, but it is unacceptable that women continue to be dismissed when presenting with the multiple common indicators of endometriosis (migraine, ibs, infertility, chronic pain from adhesions, etc…), causing most to experience decades of interconnected health issues that are never seen in a big-picture way.

comments.name: scientella
comments.body:
I was living in Australia. Had horrendous period pain.  Went to expensive private doctor who said endometriosis and I needed surgery. 
Sought a second opinion. Went to local public gyno clinic.  There they lined you up in stalls like public toilets, for privacy, but all with our legs in stirrups. One overworked doctor came along with his female assistant for legal reasons. He most unceremoniously prodded, pushed and manipulated, seeing when I screamed...or didnt in my case. 
He said "you dont have endometriosis" so saving me expensive private surgery!
And you know what...he was right.  The painful periods went away after childbirth.  So there IS a way to diagnose.  It just takes years and years and hundreds of examinations and a degree of public well meaning honesty. 

I often look back on this experience as an example of the wonders of a public health system.

comments.name: B Dawson
comments.body:
While $100 seems a bit steep, many countries charge non-residents higher fees for entrance to parks and attractions, transportation and even at restaurants.

As a non-Canadian for instance, I am required to purchase permits if I want to camp on Crown land in Ontario - a reasonable $10/night - whereas Canadians are allowed free use for 21 days at a single campsite.  Non-residents are completely excluded from Green Zones that are set aside specifically for locals, although I understand that policy is under review at the moment.

According to travel sites, it is not unusual for foreigners to be charged more at restaurants in Japan to defray the cost of translation challenges.  Egypt, India, Turkey, France are among many of countries that have differing price structures for foreigners.

I don’t see a problem with a ranked fee system.  Why shouldn’t parks and other spaces funded by government money offer lower fees to the taxpayers who support those attractions day in and day out?

As I said, $100 seems out of line and I’m intentionally not addressing the issue of whether the money is being spent to keep the parks properly managed.

We lost my beautiful nephew to suicide almost four years ago. No suicide note, at least none that I am aware of. But in the two years before he left us, his personality changed in frightening ways. His children, who he adored, were on the receiving end of ridiculous admonishments (you're brushing your teeth too loud!), he cut his parents out of his life, and told unrealistic stories about interactions with them. But, because not all were unrealistic, it was hard to know what was and wasn't real. 

After his very sudden death, a close friend revealed she had spoken to him recently, and then called his brother to say she felt strongly that something was wrong with him, and that she suspected FTP, a field in which she was working. 

My father had Alzheimer's, his father had a dementia of some kind, but no other genetic connections to FTP in our family. 

These are such powerful punches to the family unit; more than the person with the affected brain is harmed. Lives are shattered, plans are scrapped, futures are disrupted, and no one knows why until it's too late. Dementia in all its forms is world-wide health crisis, but it's mostly anecdotal education that helps people understand it. It's not enough.

comments.body: The passage the reviewer quotes is VERY reminiscent of the famous passage in Sartre's NAUSEA where Roquentin has the vision of the tree root as sheer existence. This vision is a classic locus of philosophical experience, and it is probably not duplicable, so what Mr. Akhtar is saying is not comparable; but maybe he was trying, as many have tried in the past, and failed. I taught Sartre's novel to college undergraduates, and the teaching experience always fell short, because no one who has not had an experience similar, at least, to Roquentin's, can truly make sense of the significance of an experience of existence as the "Uncarved Block" of the Tao-Te Chin. Even "Uncarved Block" has form, while Roquentin's vision did not, which made him puke. Of course, puking is not a criterion of truth: I suspect that existence may be experienced amidst overabundance joy and exhilaration, not just puking. Maybe that's what Nietzsche experienced when he described "eternal return" 6,000 fathoms beyond time and sense.

comments.name: Metaphor
comments.body:
The article states: "On Nov. 2, Mr. Diem, and his politically powerful brother, Ngo Dinh Nhu, were assassinated in a coup d’état encouraged by the United States, three weeks before the assassination of Kennedy."

In one sense that is true. But if you want to be picky about it, and I am inclined in that direction, "the United States" did not encourage the coup d’état against Diem. People did, specifically, members of the Kennedy administration.

There is a tendency to personify countries, as if they were singular individuals. Many political scientists adhere to this idea. Other political scientists, including me, prefer to see countries as made up of people. Human beings make decisions. "The United States" did not decide to topple Diem. President Kennedy and his advisors made this decision.

This is not just an academic point. Personifying governments absolves individuals of their responsibility. President Kennedy was a "cold warrior" just as much as any politician of his era. He saw the conflict in Vietnam as analogous to Korea. He thought that the government of South Vietnam could be propped up indefinitely in the face of opposition from those who wanted unification with the north. He was wrong.

comments.name: Erik Frederiksen
comments.body:
We are experiencing a very non linear increase of local and regional climate-related impacts surprising many scientists by how soon they are occurring: heat waves, droughts, wildfires, floods, stronger storms, etc.

This is in large part because ice melt, which reduces heat reflectivity, is causing the Arctic to warm around 4 times the rate of the whole planet and the decreased horizontal temperature gradient between the Arctic and the rest of the world has helped cause the northern polar jet stream to slow, and get stuck in wavy patterns.

These patterns bleed heat north and cold south, and cause weather systems to persist (like the heat wave that spread fire that incinerated Lytton, British Columbia a few years ago).

Also for every degree C rise in temperature the atmosphere can hold 7 percent more moisture, an exponential increase. Hence the “rain bombs” we’ve been seeing around the world.

As we get flooded by this from above the rate of sea level rise is accelerating and maximum storm strength is increasing.

There’s some adapting that we have to do to the changes already in the pipeline, but it wouldn’t take us long to make the changes too big to adapt to.

An interesting tradition in Japan where people tell their woes to a nandina plant:  In Japanese, the word for the nandina plant is nanten (南天). This is a homophone for a entirely different phrase, nan o tenjiru (難を転じる), which translates to "to turn difficulties into something better" or "turning misfortune into good fortune".
Because of this wordplay, a traditional custom emerged where people would literally or symbolically whisper their nightmares, worries, or grief to the nandina bushes planted in their yards. The plant acts as a spiritual vessel, conceptually absorbing the person's hardships and transforming them into good luck.   I think whether nandina or robot, sometimes venting one's troubles can be healthy and lower stress.

comments.name: Mihailo Zoin
comments.body:
Progress or Regress?

History reveals that humanity rapidly upgrades its tools while endlessly running the exact same moral and geopolitical algorithms.

Where we progressed (Institutions and self-determination):
Wyoming’s 1889 constitution and Botswana’s 1966 independence reflect genuine structural evolution toward universal suffrage and sovereignty. Rights once treated as radical territory-level experiments are now global baseline expectations.   

Where we stalled or regressed (Appeasement and bodily autonomy): The 1938 Munich Agreement remains the cautionary tale of purchasing temporary comfort with someone else’s sovereignty — a trade-off modern diplomacy still flirts with whenever authoritarian powers flex military muscle. Meanwhile, the violent repression in Iran in 2022 proves that fundamental rights are still policed by state brutality, mirroring the darkest clampdowns of the last century.   We have mastered breaking records and building systems, yet we remain alarmingly prone to repeating the fatal concessions of 1938.
